item.itunes:title: Your Windows PC has more auto-starting apps than Task Manager lets on, and you can find them in minutes
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]

The Startup tab in the Task manager is a pretty convenient way to identify any apps that launch when you sign in. It comes in pretty handy when you're trying to declutter Windows and speed up your PC. There's a catch, however. Task Manager doesn't actually show you everything that's running in the background, and believe me, there's a lot.

That's why relying exclusively on Task Manager can leave you with an incomplete picture of what's happening on your machine. If you've ever wondered why certain apps keep running despite disabling their startup entries, there's a good chance you've been looking in the wrong place.

Windows 11 has a built-in tool that handles my morning routine, and it’s better than any paid app out there

It handles all the monotonous aspects of my PC's startup routine

By  Abhishek Kumar Mishra

Task Scheduler is hiding more startup apps behind the curtain

Scheduled tasks can launch apps without ever showing up in Task Manager

Before you blame Windows for mysteriously launching background applications, the one place you must always investigate is Task Scheduler. Plenty of modern software developers have figured out that they don't need to register an application in a conventional startup location to get it running when you sign in.

Instead, they can create scheduled tasks that trigger automatically at log on, conveniently bypassing Task Manager's Startup tab. To check out the Task Scheduler, press Win + R, type taskschd.msc, and hit Enter. In the window that opens up, expand the Task Scheduler Library option on the left, and then start inspecting the tasks listed in the middle pane. Don't overlook any software-specific subfolders, either.

Here, you can double-click any suspicious entry and switch to its Triggers tab. Look for any triggers labeled At log on — that's what indicates that the task can execute whenever a user signs in. Chrome, Edge, Teams, Adobe, and OneDrive components are among the most notorious culprits here that may be using scheduled tasks for running in the background.

Do remember, though, that not every scheduled task is an unwanted startup application. Some run periodically or only when specific conditions are met. Check the Actions tab to identify what each task actually launches before disabling anything.

Should you use a Windows Task Manager alternative?

You might have heard of Task Manager alternatives for Windows 11, but should you use one?

By  Adam Conway

Not everything that launches with Windows qualifies as an app

Windows services and Startup folders have their own startup mechanisms

Task Scheduler isn't the only place where Windows hides background activity from Task Manager. Plenty of installed applications rely on Windows services to run processes independently of whether you've actually opened the associated software.

Press Win + R to bring up the Run dialog box, type services.msc, and hit Enter to open the Services console. Sort the list by Startup Type to find services configured as Automatic or Automatic (Delayed Start).

Unlike conventional startup applications, these services can start during Windows boot or shortly afterward, often without appearing in Task Manager's Startup tab. However, don't go disabling unfamiliar entries just because their names sound suspicious. Windows relies on hundreds of background services, and breaking the wrong one can cause considerably more trouble than a few extra processes.

There's also a more conventional hiding spot worth checking, which is the Startup folders. Press Win + R and enter shell: startup to inspect your personal startup folder. For entries that apply to everyone using the PC, enter shell: common startup instead. You might be surprised by what you've been overlooking.

5 Start menu alternatives and Windows tweaks that will speed up your workflow

Revamp your Windows experience with smarter Start menu alternatives and tweaks—boost efficiency, streamline navigation, and work faster

2
By  Pranav Bhardwaj

Dig a little deeper into Windows' actual startup configuration

PowerShell and Registry Editor reveal startup entries that Task Manager overlooks

Apart from doing the entirety of the digging yourself, you can also get Windows to do plenty of the investigative work for you. PowerShell has a handy command that consolidates all conventional startup entries into a nice and readable list. Run PowerShell and type in the following —

Get-CimInstance Win32_StartupCommand | Select-Object Name, Command, Location, User | Format-List

This pulls startup entries from registry Run keys and Startup folders across user and machine contexts. The Name property tells you what's launching, while the Command property tells you how it's launching. The Location and User properties help you understand which account it's associated with. If you're a single user on your PC, that last part is pretty much redundant.

Even the Registry Editor shows you exactly what's running in the background of your PC, provided you know where to look. Primarily, there are four locations inside the Registry Editor that can present a proper list of all the apps that are secretly setting themselves to auto-start with Windows. Just press Win + R and then type in regedit to open the Registry Editor, and then type in the following addresses one-by-one to see which apps try to jump over the fence without knocking at the gate first.

Computer\HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run

Computer\HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run

Computer\HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce

Computer\HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Wow6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run

From the entries that show up in these lists, you can simply pick one you don't like, or don't want starting without your express permission, and simply right-click and delete the entry. It won't delete the software from your PC, but it will stop it from booting automatically with Windows the next time you turn on your PC.

Always make sure you Export your Registry Editor backup before making any changes. With the Registry Editor open, click File > Export and save it in an accessible location.

Autoruns also shows you what Task Manager refuses to

When Windows' built-in tools aren't enough, Microsoft has already made a better one

If you want the closest thing to a complete inventory of everything that starts with Windows, Microsoft's Sysinternals Autoruns is the tool to use. This utility doesn't limit itself to just a few familiar startup locations, and actually digs through Run keys, scheduled tasks, services, drivers, Winlogon entries, Explorer extensions, and plenty of other places where software can quietly place itself.

Download and run Autoruns, then start with the Everything tab. It can look slightly terrifying at first because, well, it shows you absolutely everything. You can even go deeper and search for a specific application, properly inspect where it registered itself, and untick an entry to prevent it from launching without immediately deleting its configuration.

However, "inspect" is a pretty important word here. Autoruns exposes plenty of legitimate Windows components that you really shouldn't disable just because you don't recognize them or know what they do. If you're unsure about an entry you spot in Autoruns, then the best course of action is to check its publisher, description, image path, and VirusTotal status before touching it.

13 things you didn't know you could do with Task Manager

Level up your Task Manager knowledge

3
By  João Carrasqueira

Task Manager was never meant to be the whole story

Windows has spent years accumulating clever ways for software to make itself available on your machine. I, for one, am grateful for that convenience, but it also means that I can't just rely on the old method of "check Startup and disable what you don't need."

If your PC behaves strangely, treat startup activity like any troubleshooting problem — follow the evidence, find what is launching, and then decide whether it deserves to stay.

Once you do know where to look, though, you realize that Windows gives you the tools you need, and that's what makes the supposedly "mysterious" background activity a lot less mysterious.

item.title: I tried 5 open-source Obsidian alternatives, and one was an easy winner
item.itunes:title: I tried 5 open-source Obsidian alternatives, and one was an easy winner
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I have always had a soft spot for Obsidian. It is powerful, flexible, and offers almost endless customization. But that flexibility comes with a catch. Building the perfect workspace means spending hours configuring plugins, tweaking settings, and figuring out how to add an aesthetic touch to every corner of the vault.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

I started wondering whether there was an open-source alternative that could deliver a similarly capable experience with less effort. To find out, I tested five promising Obsidian alternatives, and among them, one app stood out from the crowd and made me reconsider my setup. That app was AppFlowy.

4 game-changing Obsidian workflows I wish I tried earlier

Obsidian workflows I tried late, but you don’t have to

4
By  Parth Shah

Five open-source alternatives entered my testing

Each app brought something different

I didn’t want to settle for the first promising Obsidian alternative, so I shortlisted five open-source apps with different approaches to note-taking and productivity. I started with Logseq, which felt familiar thanks to its backlinks, knowledge graphs, and connected notes.

However, I wasn’t a fan of its outline-first approach, which required a learning curve.

Next was Joplin, a straightforward note-taking app with Markdown support, notebooks, and synchronization options. It handled the basics well, but I found its overall experience somewhat limited.

TriliumNext was another interesting contender, especially for its powerful hierarchical organization and advanced knowledge management features. However, its interface felt a little overwhelming.

SiYuan impressed me with its block references, databases, and extensive built-in functionality. It was easily among the stronger contenders. But I wasn’t a fan of its UX. Also, the Mac app felt rough on the edges.

Finally, I explored AppFlowy, which took a different approach by combining note-taking, databases, and project management in a modern workspace. I tested all five with everyday notes, tasks, and project workflows. While each had its strengths, AppFlowy clearly matched my requirements better than the others.

AppFlowy immediately grabbed my attention

More than just another note-taking app

Of all the Obsidian alternatives I tested, AppFlowy made the strongest first impression. The moment I launched it, I was greeted by a clean, modern interface that felt more like a complete productivity workspace than a traditional note-taking app.

The sidebar neatly organizes my pages and workspaces, while the block-based editor makes creating and formatting content effortless. I could quickly add headings, checklists, tables, and other elements without switching between menus.

AppFlowy felt intuitive to use. With Obsidian, I often spend a good chunk of time installing plugins, adjusting settings, and customizing my vault to match my workflow. AppFlowy takes a different approach by offering several essential productivity features right out of the box.

I could create nested pages, organize my documents, and build a structured workspace without much initial configuration. Even the small details like the icons, menus, and page layouts look polished, and navigating between different sections feels natural.

Built-in databases changed everything

Project management became effortless

One of the biggest reasons I chose AppFlowy was its database functionality. I have used Obsidian Bases to organize information, but AppFlowy takes it further with a more visual, intuitive approach. I could create databases, add custom properties, filter entries, and switch between different views without much effort. Everything felt neatly integrated into the workspace.

For example, I created a database to manage my editorial workflow. I added columns for articles, publication dates, priority levels, and current status. I could use the grid view to see everything at a glance or switch to a Kanban board to visualize how my articles are progressing.

I could maintain detailed notes about an article and manage its progress within the same workspace. Obsidian can handle simple workflows with Bases and community plugins, but I found AppFlowy’s approach more natural for managing projects.

Months into Obsidian, I finally discovered features I should've used from day one

Powerful features were hiding in plain sight

By  Patrick Hearn

AppFlowy is packed with features

It’s a complete workspace

The more time I spent with AppFlowy, the more impressed I became with its extensive feature set. It offers templates that help you get started in no time. I also like the Slash command, where I can format my sentences and paragraphs in no time.

AppFlowy also comes with AI capabilities to help with writing, summarizing information, and organizing ideas. I can use its AI-powered tools to speed up repetitive tasks, although some functionality depends on the plan and setup.

Another thoughtful addition is Google Drive integration. I can embed relevant Drive files directly into my pages instead of constantly switching between applications.

The database features go beyond traditional tables and Kanban boards, too. AppFlowy supports charts for visualizing data, alongside timeline views for planning projects and tracking deadlines.

A fresh approach to managing everything

Logseq, Joplin, TrilliumNext, and SiYuan all have their strengths, but AppFlowy stood out for me. Its polished interface, built-in databases, flexible Kanban boards, and project management capabilities make it much more than a simple note-taking app.

It brings everything together without requiring dozens of plugins. AppFlowy isn’t perfect, and Obsidian still has the upper hand in certain areas, but if you are looking for an open-source productivity workspace that goes beyond managing notes, AppFlowy deserves a serious look.

item.title: Before GTA VI comes out, I'm playing the entirety of GTA V completely in my web browser
item.itunes:title: Before GTA VI comes out, I'm playing the entirety of GTA V completely in my web browser
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
With Grand Theft Auto VI just days away, it's astonishing that GTA V is still coming up with brand-new ways to play. Over the past few months, it's striking how the boundaries of PC gaming have become increasingly arbitrary.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Browser-based games are all the rage today, especially with the barrage of AAA ports that are flooding Chrome and Firefox. And yet, nothing could have prepared me for having Grand Theft Auto V running in a browser tab.

Somehow, all it took to start playing one of the greatest AAA games ever made was opening a new tab in Chrome and waiting a few minutes.

The game just runs, and I wasn't expecting that

This is so much more than a glorified browser demo

I've tested my fair share of browser-based game projects, so I went into this one expecting the usual compromises. Truth be told, I fully expected to be able to play just a small section of Los Santos, with maybe a handful of playable mechanics. Instead, GTA V loaded up with surprisingly little fuss, and I found myself staring at an experience that felt considerably closer to the real thing.

In fact, the initial process was shockingly frictionless. Within a couple of minutes, I was playing the actual campaign. This wasn't a decoy or rip-off, either — Michael, Trevor, and the gang were fully storming the bank and escaping the police as I played through the entire GTA V prologue. I even expected the game to cut out or loop on itself after the prologue, but minutes later, I was playing as Franklin, repossessing cars and driving around a tow truck.

There's even a sandbox mode, and it dropped me straight into a random section of Los Santos, giving me a full stack of weapons, cheats, and the freedom to explore the entire map. That was particularly useful, too, since nothing clears your head like loading up the sandbox mode and blowing up anything that moves with a grenade launcher and God Mode turned on.

Ultimately, though, having this option available through a browser tab is still difficult to wrap my head around. After getting over the sheer novelty of running GTA V in a browser, one of the first things I noticed was how familiar everything felt. The keyboard controls were exactly what I'd expect from the Windows PC version, with no awkward remapping or bizarre input behavior getting between Los Santos and me.

My muscle memory, built over thirteen years, kicked in almost immediately. Getting my controller working was equally painless. I plugged in my DualSense, and had Windows recognize it as an Xbox controller (DS4Windows starts at boot). From there, everything worked as expected, including the familiar button mappings.

AI-created gaming mod mashups are pure chaos, and I can't get enough of them

Tommy Vercetti is the new Tony Hawk

By  Samarveer Singh

There are bugs and glitches, but it's hard to care

Los Santos in Google Chrome still throws up some hiccups

Of course, getting GTA V running in a browser doesn't mean every part of the experience is perfect. Throughout my time playing, I kept running into graphical oddities. It was easy to ignore the occasional missing road texture since I could just drive away, but it was much more immersion-breaking when I entered a full area with zero building textures and roads floating an inch above my car.

Clearly, GTA V on a web browser is pretty buggy — cars in traffic were popping in and out of thin air, and some were driving while halfway embedded in the road. At times, it almost felt like playing Cyberpunk 2077 at release in 2020. Of course, this was much more forgivable, since this was still a proper AAA game that I could close by pressing Ctrl+W in my browser.

Thankfully, most of these issues weren't persistent. Respawning my character usually brought missing assets back into place, although having to deliberately die to fix graphical glitches isn't exactly my idea of troubleshooting.

What was even more surprising was that the game also offered graphics settings, instead of locking me into whatever configuration the browser port considered appropriate. I could monitor GPU utilization and VRAM consumption while playing, too, which made for an interesting hardware experiment.

Curiously, GTA V in the web browser actually took up around 6 GB of VRAM from my RTX 4070 Ti, all while my GPU utilization never crossed 20%. The whole time, though, it ran at a smooth 60 FPS, no matter how much I cranked up the in-game settings.

Ranking all 12 GTA games from worst to best

Answering the question: "which GTA did it best?"

13
By  Yousef A. Zain

No GTA Online, but I don't mind

A browser tab is all I need to cause some mayhem

Over the past decade, GTA V's online multiplayer has arguably been the main reason for its continued success and why it remains as relevant as ever today. That's the one significant omission from this browser-based GTA V experience. You can't jump into GTA Online like you can if you played the original Halo: Combat Evolved in a browser. This is strictly a single-player affair.

And yet, I still don't think that takes away from what makes this project so impressive. GTA V's single-player sandbox has always been entertaining enough to warrant revisiting, even when you've exhausted its campaign and have absolutely no interest in completing another mission.

What really gets me is how accessible the whole thing is. You don't need to download dozens of gigabytes, configure an emulator, or spend an afternoon troubleshooting compatibility issues. There's also the rather awkward question of legality. These browser-based ports operate in a legal grey area, particularly when they rely on reverse-engineered code and original game assets.

This one, though, is clearly illegal, and there are no two ways about it. Rockstar certainly hasn't authorized anyone to distribute GTA V through a browser link, so you should expect this project to become inaccessible any time now.

That said, the open-source nature of some of these projects means clones and mirrors could surface almost as quickly (if not faster) as the original disappears. Enjoy the novelty while it lasts, because I wouldn't count on this particular link staying alive forever.

Rockstar reportedly responds to plea from terminally ill fan to play GTA VI early

The "huge GTA fan" reportedly won't make it to the anticipated game's release.

27
By  Patrick O'Rourke

That's another platform for GTA V before GTA VI comes out

It's almost poetic how just days before Grand Theft Auto VI finally comes out, the previous entry, which remains Rockstar's biggest cash cow today, is perfectly playable for free inside a browser. In fact, some would say that Rockstar and Sony started this landslide of PC ports and decompilations in the first place, with the former deciding to forgo a physical disc release for GTA VI and the latter going all-digital for all post-2028 games.

I, for one, can't wait to boot up Jason and Lucia's adventure in GTA VI, come November 19. In the meantime, though, a single new tab in Chrome or Firefox will help me pay my respects and bid goodbye to Los Santos, the city that's been a playground for millions of players for the past thirteen years.

item.itunes:title: My gaming GPU sat idle most of the day, so I turned it into a local AI server the whole house can use
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
It'll likely come as no surprise to anyone well-versed in PC hardware that a GPU spends most of its life doing almost nothing. It only springs into action when you launch a game, render a scene in Blender, or fire up a simulator. When your job revolves around juggling documents and Excel spreadsheets like mine, that means most of the time the GPU just sits in its PCIe slot, waiting for the weekend.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

With the hardware that I have in my rig, I already knew that I could turn my RTX 4070 Ti Super-equipped PC into a dedicated AI server for my home and bring Qwen3.6-35B-A3B to every other device that I have under the roof, none of which could hope to run it natively. What I didn't know, though, was just how easy llama.cpp would make it. Here's how I'm serving the best model I can run on my 16GB GPU to the whole house, and how little it takes to do so.

The entire setup took one command

Llama.cpp's built-in web UI turned every device in the house into a client

If you've been following my work, you'd know that I prefer llama.cpp over any other runtime for local AI inference because of the customizability and performance it offers. I've already got a recent build (b11927) set up, along with the model file for my model of choice, which is Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (which is a UD-IQ4_XS quant from Unsloth) which I use for various purposes on my PC.

The two are the only prerequisites for serving local AI from your PC, and if you've already got a similar build and a model you'd like to serve, the only thing to do is run one command in PowerShell:

llama-server -m "C:\path\to\your-model.gguf" --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080

Now, naturally, you'd have to replace the path with the path to your own model, which is wherever you have saved the model's GGUF file. For example, for me, serving Qwen3.6-35B-A3B would mean running the following script:

llama-server - m "C:\llama.cpp\models\Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-IQ4_XS.gguf" --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080

The specific flag here that makes it a server is --host 0.0.0.0, which instructs llama-server to listen on your home network instead of only on your PC as you would normally do. On the other hand, --port 8080 pins the port, since llama.cpp plans to move its default to 9931 in a future release (which is a point it makes every time you load a model). Everything else can stay at llama.cpp's defaults which, conveniently enough, already split the context into slots, so several users can chat at once and fit the model into your free VRAM on their own.

I ditched cloud AI for these 3 local models, and my 8GB GPU handles them all

8GB may not be great for games, but it can be more than enough for these local models

1
By  Abhinav Raj

But how "fast" do the models run on the client?

About as "fast" and as well as they run on the host

The reason why llama.cpp is perfect for setting up a home AI server is because you barely lose anything in terms of performance against the baseline measured on your host. This is because the model never really leaves your PC. Llama-server does the inference on the GPU and streams the reply back as plain text, one token at a time.

Even at 90 tokens per second, that's only a fraction of a megabit per second, which any home Wi-Fi network is equipped to handle easily. This is slightly different from a game streaming server like those reliant on Sunshine and Moonlight since game streaming has to send every frame as video, while this server only sends words. As a result, whatever speed the host generates at is the speed the client gets, after a few milliseconds of delay before the first word shows up on the browser.

The reason why I can claim this is because I brought the numbers with me. For my own testing, I tuned the command for my RTX 4070 Ti Super, Ryzen 5 7600X and 32GB of DDR5 using specific flags to optimize the performance. Have a look at this command:

llama-server -m "C:\llama.cpp\models\Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-IQ4_XS.gguf" --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 -ngl 99 --n-cpu-moe 8 -c 32768 -np 2 -kvu -fa on --load-mode none

As Qwen3.6-35B-A3B is about 17.7GB against my 16GB of VRAM, I use --n-cpu-moe 8 to offload the expert weights of the model's first eight layers to system RAM, whereas -ngl 99 keeps everything else resident on the VRAM itself.

During inference with the specific MoE model, only about 3 billion of its 35 billion params are active, which is why splitting the experts between VRAM and RAM keeps it fast. For my use, I keep the context window set to 32K, and -np 2 gives the server two chat slots so two people can use it at once. The -kvu flag lets both slots share that context.

item.itunes:title: Claude Code wrote the Windows setup script I kept putting off, and my fresh installs now finish in 20 minutes
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Every time I install a fresh copy of Windows, I go through pretty much the same ritual. First, I install a browser (I like Brave) because I don't want to use anything Microsoft shoves in my face. Next, I download a slew of everyday applications, toggle off all the annoying settings Windows enables by default, and remove the remaining bloat.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

I've always known that a setup script would be the best answer to automating this. But that means chasing down a bunch of PowerShell commands, winget app IDs, and registry edits, then compiling it all into a script. It sounded like tedious work, so it stayed low on my to-do list. Then, I decided to let Claude Code tackle the job for me. Now I have a PowerShell script that sets up a new Windows install just the way I like it in only a few minutes, and I no longer have to remember all the little settings I'd ordinarily tweak.

I used Claude Code to control apps that weren't built for AI, and it opens up a whole new workflow

Time to give my apps a new operator

1
By  Mahnoor Faisal

Finding the right commands is the worst part

But Claude Code made that look easy

I didn't add much preamble to my prompt to Claude. I just opened the window and started listing the settings and features I like in a newly installed Windows system. The list was split into the apps I normally install, the Explorer tweaks I make every time, the features I always disable, and a request for a nicer-looking terminal. Claude returned a single PowerShell script divided into sections, which makes it easy to comment out any part I decide not to use. It also checks before making changes, so running it more than once won't hurt anything. A summary at the end gives a breakdown of everything it did.

The scripting itself isn't that big of a deal. The part of this that I never had the patience for was researching what to include inside the script. Claude checked online to get the right package IDs for winget and to find out which registry values needed to be set. Some things could be changed with a simple PowerShell command, so it collected that info too. The only part of the script that's not straightforward is the WSL install. That step requires a reboot, then the script uses a RunOnce entry to pick up where it left off.

Everything the script does to Windows

App installs, WSL, and numerous tweaks

Apps get installed before anything else is done. Winget installs the common stuff I use almost every day, like Notepad++, Brave web browser, 7-Zip, VLC, Everything (file search), VS Code, PowerToys, and about a dozen more things. That's achieved with a simple loop:

$apps = 'Notepad++.Notepad++','7zip.7zip','VideoLAN.VLC','BraveSoftware.BraveBrowser'
foreach ($id in $apps) { winget install -e --id $id --silent --accept-package-agreements --accept-source-agreements }

The -e flag makes the winget search strict about matching the exact package ID I typed. That's important because I want to ensure that I'm getting the official app and not something similar. The other few flags minimize the prompts I receive during installation.

Next up is what essentially amounts to a handful of registry edits. That's the typical way that various settings are toggled on or off in Windows. I have it doing things like turning on dark mode system-wide, showing hidden files and known file extensions, opening Explorer to This PC by default, and confirming before sending a file to the Recycle Bin. One command per registry value does the trick, but Claude also uses variables for parts that repeat:

$adv = 'HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\Advanced'
Set-ItemProperty $adv Hidden 1; Set-ItemProperty $adv HideFileExt 0; Set-ItemProperty $adv LaunchTo 1

The next part of the script is the debloat section. It removes all the things about Windows that annoy me, including but not limited to: Copilot, Recall, Bing results in Start menu, widgets, and Start menu recommendations. After that, the script wraps up with a few terminal settings and installing WSL. After rebooting, Ubuntu opens so I can finish setting that up myself, since it's the only part that requires my input.

Be careful about what you let AI change

Don't blindly run a dozen registry edits without checking

Keep in mind that editing the wrong registry keys or executing unknown PowerShell commands can have disastrous results. Treat the PowerShell script Claude spits out the same way you treat scripts you find on Windows forums: with an abundance of caution. A new update could also render some commands in the script obsolete, so check the logs after the script runs.

Since PowerShell scripts are written in plain text, it's easy to check the commands against online documentation. I had Claude Code cite its sources for everything it wrote, which made double-checking its work trivial. If you're on Pro, using Windows Sandbox to test out the script first would be the best way to verify that it works as intended.

One script does my whole setup

I'd always wanted a script like this, and handing off the task to Claude Code is what finally got it built. Without it, it'd likely be sitting perpetually on my to-do list. If you want to streamline your setup process, consider Claude Code a good partner to help you get it done.

item.title: Zelda: Ocarina of Time reportedly already runs on PC through an emulator, just hours after its Switch 2 release
item.itunes:title: Zelda: Ocarina of Time reportedly already runs on PC through an emulator, just hours after its Switch 2 release
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The anticipated Switch 2 remake of N64 classic The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is already sort of playable on PC through emulators, just hours after its November 5th release — yes, you read that correctly.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Switch 2 emulation is still very much in its infancy, with games like Mario Kart World and Donkey Kong Bonanza (Splatoon Raiders barely boots) running at varied frame rates on PC through emulators like Eglantine, a fork of a Switch 2-focused version of the Switch emulator Eden, and Lichii, which is actually a fork of Eglantine. Of course, all of this follows the Switch 2 being jailbroken last month.

Confused yet? Don't worry — me too. A lot has happened in the space in a short time. Progress on these projects is moving surprisingly quickly thanks to AI tools like Claude. A quick scroll in certain corners of social media reveals countless other forks of both emulators, with creators competing for the glory of getting Zelda: Ocarina of Time running smoothly on PC through emulation.

When it comes to the Ocarina of Time Switch 2 remake, Lichii seems to be making the most progress, with the game running between 15fps and 30fps (the game plays at 60fps on the Switch 2), depending on how powerful your hardware is. There's even an example of someone getting the game to run at nearly 60fps with Lichii inside the Great Deku Tree with an RTX 5080 and a Ryzen 7 9800X3D.

The relatively solid frame rate is likely because this is a small area in the game, and I bet it slows to a crawl in Hyrule Field. Still, it's impressive to see in action.

I wouldn't be surprised to see Zelda: Ocarina of Time in a more playable state on PC soon

Switch 2 PC emulation is moving at a fast pace

Ocarina of Time remake emulation on PC still seems full of visual glitches and, overall, a bit of a mess. In some clips I've seen, players can't even get out of the game's starting area. Still, it's surprising to see the game running on PC this quickly, and Nintendo likely isn't very happy about it.

While earlier Lichii builds could barely run Zelda: Ocarina of Time, build 75 includes several performance improvements, including 80 previously unsupported shaders, allowing more environments to render correctly. Zortos293, the project's developer, says there are still many issues to iron out, including too much fog, overexposed lighting, and overall poor performance.

To play Zelda: Ocarina of Time on PC with an emulator, you need to legally own a copy of the title and dump it into a compatible file format from your jailbroken Switch 2. I also haven't tried playing the game through Lichii myself, so I can't verify the emulator footage that's been share online. However, it looks very legitimate to me.

In other AI-assisted gaming project-related news, Anthropic seems to have introduced an instruction telling Claude not to recreate specific existing games, even if they're renamed, which could limit the explosive growth the retro and modern PC port space has seen over the past few weeks.

One of the first public Switch 2 emulators is already running Mario Kart World shockingly well

Nintendo likely isn't happy about this.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

item.title: I spent $500 to upgrade my aging gaming PC, and it beat buying a new one
item.itunes:title: I spent $500 to upgrade my aging gaming PC, and it beat buying a new one
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When I got a new gaming PC in 2022, my old system sat gathering dust for a few years. As I got busy with work and gaming on my new rig, upgrading the older PC was forgotten. Ever since the PC hardware market was hit by drastic price hikes last year, the idea of reviving my older machine had become even less feasible — GPUs, SSDs, and memory had become out of reach.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Lately, however, I felt the need for a second gaming rig for my TV. I had recently added a home theater system, and wanted to experience immersive gaming in the entertainment room. Moving my main PC wasn't an option, and streaming had its own issues. Buying an overpriced console was a non-starter, too, so I got to work on making the most of what I already had — upgrading my older PC with a $500 budget.

4 free yet game-changing upgrades I made to my ancient PC

I got a bigger performance boost than I expected

6
By  Tanveer Singh

My first-gen Ryzen PC was clearly outclassed

It was great while it lasted

To be fair, expecting too much from my 2017 gaming rig was inhuman. After all, it was built on the Ryzen 5 1600, the first 6-core chip from AMD's revived lineup. Although I had replaced my original GPU with a GTX 1660 Ti in 2019, it couldn't keep up with the AAA games released in 2022, let alone 2026. Even at 1080p, I had to make far too many compromises to the graphics settings to get playable framerates.

To add to its troubles, the PC only had 16GB of DDR4 RAM rated for 3,000 MT/s, so I was right at the edge of what could be termed "enough" for modern gaming. I wasn't going to be content with a secondary PC that supported retro and older titles; I wanted a proper gaming experience on my 50-inch TV. I had to have a PC capable of at least some of the newer upscaling techniques, if not all.

Buying a current-gen graphics card would have exhausted my $500 budget on the GPU alone, and I would have managed only an RTX 5060. It would have been twice as fast as my GTX 1660 Ti, but I wouldn't have had anything left to spend on any other component. Even after adding a current-gen GPU, my rig would have been held back.

Connecting a desktop to my TV was the best choice I ever made

When I ended up with two working desktop gaming PCs and only one monitor, I decided to get creative.

13
By  Madeline Ricchiuto

A single CPU or GPU upgrade wouldn't cut it, so I bought both

I even managed to squeeze in a 32GB memory kit

  • Credit: Remedy Entertainment
  • Credit: Remedy Entertainment

I figured that instead of prioritizing any one area of the build, I could upgrade everything if I only looked at the pre-owned market. Considering what the PC hardware market is going through, used components are probably the only source of respite left for builders and upgraders alike. So, I went hunting for deals on previous-gen GPUs and CPUs, trying to fit everything within $500.

I already had the RTX 3080 in mind for its excellent price-to-performance, decent VRAM capacity, and enough DLSS support to make not just 1080p but even 1440p gaming possible. I found many listings for the RTX 3080 10GB ranging from around $280 to $350, and grabbed one at the lower end. For $280, a two-generation-old high-end GPU was a sweet deal. It was almost thrice as fast as the GTX 1660 Ti, offering me a great uplift for the price.

Since I had a lot of my budget to spare, I could afford to buy a more powerful AM4 CPU. The Ryzen 5 5600 was available brand-new for around $150, but I could buy it on the used market for just $100. The Zen 3 processor was twice as fast as my Ryzen 5 1600 in gaming, so I welcomed the savings and secured the deal, leaving around $100 on my self-imposed $500 budget.

My 16GB RAM was starting to look even older, now that I could replace it with a 32GB pre-owned kit rated at 3,600 MT/s. It cost me just under $100 and allowed me to avoid the stability and reliability issues from mixing old and new kits. The 32GB RAM made my old PC relatively future-proof, as newer titles would have caused problems with 16GB of memory.

From barely clearing 60 FPS at 1080p, my new setup was cruising at 100+ FPS at 4K Medium/High settings in nearly every modern title, thanks to a massive generational uplift and DLSS upscaling. Whether it was Cyberpunk 2077, Black Myth: Wukong, or Resident Evil Requiem, I wasn't missing out on anything. Ray tracing wasn't in the picture on my 4K TV, but I was content with the night-and-day difference between my previous rig and the new one.

4 AM4 CPUs you don't need to replace yet in 2025

Don't rush into an upgrade if your rig is running one of these

56
By  Abhinav Raj

Upgrading an old PC doesn't need current-gen hardware

There are many steps in between

While upgrades mean jumping to something newer, it doesn't have to be the latest and greatest hardware, especially in a market heavily stacked against gamers. I would have considered a better GPU had the market been in a different place. However, I needed to work with the hand I was dealt, and I did the best I could in my $500 budget.

Spending more than that, even in a sane market, would have been lavish, considering I wasn't upgrading my main PC. For a machine dedicated to TV gaming, I wasn't going to empty my wallet. Jumping from a GTX 1660 Ti to an RTX 3080 was a great upgrade for less than $300, and the Ryzen 5 5600 for $100 prevented a CPU bottleneck.

The upgrade allowed me to transition from 1080p to upscaled 4K gaming on a massive screen. So, I'm not complaining too much about the market. I won't need to spend anything on my second PC anytime soon. As for my main PC, I'm still waiting to upgrade my RTX 3080 to another high-end GPU. When I'll be able to do that is anyone's guess — well, maybe Sam Altman or Jensen Huang know better.

Why I'd buy a two-generation-old flagship GPU before any new mid-range card

You get better value.

17
By  Anurag Singh

Buying older-gen parts on the used market is underrated

Most people don't want to risk buying faulty hardware from the pre-owned market, but you can find safe deals while saving money if you know what to look for. Buying from reputable sellers and ensuring you have buyer protection on the platform you're using are enough to trust pre-owned components. It can save you hundreds without compromising on performance.

I figured that instead of prioritizing any one area of the build, I could upgrade everything if I only looked at the pre-owned market. Considering what the PC hardware market is going through, used components are probably the only source of respite left for builders and upgraders alike. So, I went hunting for deals on previous-gen GPUs and CPUs, trying to fit everything within $500.

I already had the RTX 3080 in mind for its excellent price-to-performance, decent VRAM capacity, and enough DLSS support to make not just 1080p but even 1440p gaming possible. I found many listings for the RTX 3080 10GB ranging from around $280 to $350, and grabbed one at the lower end. For $280, a two-generation-old high-end GPU was a sweet deal. It was almost thrice as fast as the GTX 1660 Ti, offering me a great uplift for the price.

item.title: I ditched Claude Code's desktop app for its open-source rival that does the same jobs for free
item.itunes:title: I ditched Claude Code's desktop app for its open-source rival that does the same jobs for free
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Claude Code's desktop app has had a busy year. Anthropic redesigned it earlier in the year and is still adding new features. For anyone who prefers to click buttons rather than type commands, this is probably the friendliest way to work with an agent and hand it a folder of files. It does come with a catch, which is that everything runs on Anthropic's terms.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

OpenCode has always been the obvious open-source alternative, but its reputation comes from the terminal, and that's a hard sell for visual workers who just want buttons. As reluctant as I was to the terminal at first, that's where I've been using it and I've gotten used to it. But I was a little late to the party because it turns out OpenCode has had a desktop app for a while now, and naturally, that's where I started handling my work. And it's actually a really strong Claude Code desktop rival.

I tested Claude Code against 3 open-source alternatives, and one came surprisingly close

Claude might not be the only coding agent worth using.

8
By  Anurag Singh

The problem with Claude Code on desktop

Where it starts to pinch

Claude Code on desktop lives inside the Claude app as the Code tab, so it's right by your regular chats and every other surface Anthropic has to offer instead of being its own app. It's also only on paid plans, starting with Pro at $20 a month, which was fine for me because I'm already paying for Pro.

The bigger issue for me is that it only runs Claude. Even the desktop app's third-party mode only accepts gateways that serve Claude models, so a dull chore like renaming a folder of files still goes to Claude when one of the models on my own GPU could honestly handle it. Every one of those chores comes out of the same usage pool as my chats, so a tidy-up in the Code tab can eat into conversations I wanted to have later in the week.

Taking that subscription elsewhere isn't an option either. Anthropic blocks Pro and Max subscriptions from working in third-party tools, so the plan only pays off if I stay inside Anthropic's own apps.

I use OpenCode over Claude Code, and it's every bit as good

Beat-for-beat, feature-for-feature.

9
By  Mahnoor Faisal

OpenCode has a desktop app now

I spent weeks in the terminal for no good reason

Only up until recently, my OpenCode use happened in the terminal because I didn't know it had a desktop app. The terminal is a little outside my comfort zone, but it was surprisingly easy to get used to. Shortly after I started using it, though, I discovered the desktop app through doing research for another OpenCode article. Turns out, the app was released in beta almost a year ago for Windows, macOS, and Linux, so I somehow just completely missed its existence.

It's changed quite a bit since then. In July, OpenCode finished moving the desktop app to a new layout with browser-style tabs for each session. OpenCode 2.0 came out in October with even more changes, so there's now one background service that the terminal, web, and desktop apps all connect to. The desktop app is running the same agent as the terminal version.

The cool thing about OpenCode is that it gives you a bunch of appearance customizations, whereas Claude Code barely does. The Appearance page lets you pick light, dark, or system mode, and the interface, code, and terminal each get their own font field. OpenCode 2.2.0 went further at the end of October with desktop plugins, which can add their own panels and styling to the app. There's a long list of themes to pick from if you want to apply something immediately and people are already building full themes of their own.

I run OpenCode with a different model for every job, and I haven't hit a rate limit yet

I stopped leaning on one model for everything

By  Nolen Jonker

OpenCode supports my entire workflow pipeline

It turned out to be more of a workspace than a coding agent

Model choice is probably the main reason to pick OpenCode over Claude, regardless of whether you're in the desktop app or the terminal. The composer has a model picker on every prompt, so most chores go to one of my local models from LM Studio, but I can still plug in a Claude model whenever the job calls for it. Also, OpenCode's own free models are in the same list when I don't want to load anything. The mix of local and cloud API is ideal in my opinion, and it also means that I can use Claude at a lower cost because API rates work out to less than half of the monthly subscription.

My skills came over too. OpenCode automatically checks the same skills folder Claude Code uses, so the ones I'd built for my workflows and folders show up without me having to set up anything, and you just call them by typing @. Project instructions work differently though. OpenCode 2.0 only reads AGENTS.md now, so anything sitting in a CLAUDE.md file would need to be copied across.

The built-in browser is what makes the app feel more like a workspace to me. It opens as a tab in the side panel with Ctrl+Alt+B, and the agent can drive it without me. When I ask it to check the habit tracker I vibe coded, for example, it opens the page and reads the console errors itself instead of me copying them over.

MCP servers are where the GUI runs out for now. You can connect and sign in to them inside the app with /mcps, but adding one in the first place still means a terminal command or a config file, which seems like an odd thing to ask of the people a desktop app is for, but maybe it's still on the way.

I ditched Claude Cowork for a free open-source alternative, and I'm getting more done

Cowork set the bar, but it doesn't own the idea

1
By  Nolen Jonker

One app for the boring jobs, another for the big ones

OpenCode's desktop app only just got out of beta, but it already handles all the basics I waste my Claude usage on. Claude Code's app feels more polished to me, and I still keep it around for bigger jobs where I want Opus on my subscription. Even though OpenCode's GUI gives you more in terms of workspace features after its updates, its selling point is still the ability to mix and match pretty much any model out there right now, ranging from free to the lower costs of API rates.
